stimulus.text:
John Quincy Adams, diary, January 10, 1820, writing as Secretary of State during the Missouri crisis:

“I take it for granted that the present question is a mere preamble—a title-page to a great tragic volume. ... The President thinks this question will be winked away by a compromise. But so do not I. Much am I mistaken if it is not destined to survive his political and individual life and mine.”

Background: The Missouri Compromise, admitting Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, was completed in Congress in March 1820.
stimulus.source_note: Quotation verbatim from John Quincy Adams, diary, January 10, 1820, Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, vol. 5, public domain.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from John Quincy Adams, diary, January 10, 1820, public domain

parts.prompt: Briefly identify ONE claim Adams makes in the passage about the Missouri question.
parts.modelAnswer: Adams claims the Missouri question is only a preamble, a title page to a great tragic volume. He says it will outlive both President Monroe and himself.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for naming one claim the passage makes, such as the Missouri question being only a preamble, or its outliving Monroe and Adams.
scoring.notEarned: Naming a claim the passage does not make does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE reason Adams doubted the compromise would settle the question.
parts.modelAnswer: Adams doubted the compromise because it settled only Missouri, while the underlying fight over slavery's spread would return with each new territory. A bargain over one state could not end a conflict rooted in the whole country.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one reason for Adams's doubt, such as the compromise settling one state while the slavery question remained, or the fight returning with new territories.
scoring.notEarned: Restating Adams's claim without explaining why he doubted the compromise does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE limitation of the passage as evidence about how most Americans viewed the Missouri crisis.
parts.modelAnswer: Adams was one man, the Secretary of State, writing privately in his diary. His passage shows his own fear, not what most Americans, North or South, thought about the crisis.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one limit, such as Adams writing as one elite official in a private diary rather than speaking for most Americans.
scoring.notEarned: Saying the passage is one-sided without naming whose view it leaves out does not earn the point.
